## TL;DR

I made the shared toast announcements less disruptive and more specific for assistive technology. The toast container is now a named, polite, non-atomic notifications region. Each error toast remains urgent through its own alert role, while success and informational messages use status roles. Dismiss controls identify the message they dismiss. A component regression test pins those choices. The app built, headless Chromium mounted the no-auth dashboard without uncaught page errors, and the focused UI/store tests passed. The required changed-path RepoOS check is the final verification step.

## Work and rationale

The task calls out notifications, toasts, banners and dismissals as a broad QA area. I started with the shared `ToastPanel.vue` because it is the single app-wide surface used by many independent actions and errors. Its previous live-region configuration applied `aria-live="assertive"` and `aria-atomic="true"` to the entire list. That means a mutation to the list can ask a screen reader to interrupt the current reading and replay all toast content as a single atomic update. With up to five messages stacked, dismissing one could re-announce messages that had already been heard. This conflicts with the intended clear and non-stale notification experience.

I changed the container to a named region, “Notifications”, with polite announcements and `aria-atomic="false"`. This makes the stack discoverable without forcing every update to replay all contents. A toast gets an individual live role based on its type: errors are alerts because they need prompt attention, and successes or informational messages are statuses. The close button’s accessible name now includes the corresponding toast text, so users navigating by controls can understand what will be removed without first locating adjacent content.

I added `toast-panel-a11y.test.ts` to exercise the rendered component with both a success and an error. It checks the region name and live-region settings, each per-toast role, and the contextual dismiss name. Existing Repo store tests cover deduplication, manual removal, six-second expiry, and error routing; I ran those alongside the new test to check the change against the underlying toast lifecycle.

The QA note records this as a targeted pass rather than claiming to have reviewed every notification source and page banner. The product has many inline errors with their own lifetimes and roles. I did not make broad semantics changes to those surfaces without a reproducible finding, since they express different states and often keep important error context visible until the next action.

## Approaches tried

I read the task specification, inspected the toast component, the store’s `pushToast` and `removeToast` lifecycle, and the existing store tests. I used the existing shared component instead of adjusting every caller, because the announcement behavior is centralized there. I added a component-level test rather than asserting only on store state; the accessibility regression is in the rendered markup, so the test needs to observe the semantics users and assistive technology receive.

For browser QA, I built the UI and started the requested auth-less dev server from this task worktree. Port 7272 was already in use, so I selected 7382 rather than disturbing the existing listener. A headless Playwright Chromium page loaded the RepoOS title and dashboard content at 390 × 844. It reported no page exceptions. The live app did not naturally emit a toast during initial load, so I did not represent that shell check as proof of interactive dismissal; the component regression and store tests cover those separate behaviors.

## Challenges and blockers

This is a broad QA task, but the reproducible issue found in the shared notification surface was specific: overly assertive, atomic announcements and an ambiguous dismiss label. I limited implementation to that cross-app defect and documented which other surfaces were not audited. This avoids turning a focused accessibility correction into a speculative rewrite of many page-level banners.

The default no-auth port was occupied. I left it untouched and ran this worktree’s server on 7382, then stopped the process with its own session interrupt after browser inspection. The build printed existing dependency externalization and large-chunk advisories, but completed successfully. The full RepoOS check remains authoritative for changed-path formatting, typechecking, tests and smoke verification.

## Key learnings

Live-region settings on a list affect every update to that list, not just the newly inserted message. For a toast stack, atomic announcements can create redundant speech and assertive announcements can interrupt the user even when a message is only informational. Applying urgency per toast allows errors to stay prominent while routine outcomes remain polite. Dismiss controls should identify the item they act on, particularly when several identical icon buttons are stacked.

The browser shell check and component test answer different questions. Headless Playwright verified that the built app served and mounted in the isolated no-auth environment; it did not imply a toast had appeared. The component test directly verified rendered accessibility attributes, while store tests verified lifecycle behavior. Keeping the QA note explicit about these boundaries makes the evidence reproducible and avoids overstating coverage.
